questions.prompt: A lead compensator is placed near the intended crossover so that
options: its phase bump sits where \(|L|\) crosses 1
the low-frequency gain becomes infinite without a phase change
a right-half-plane zero is cancelled by the new pole
the crossover frequency is guaranteed not to move
questions.explanation: The peak lead sits at the geometric mean of the zero and the pole. That is the frequency where you want \(|L| = 1\), because phase margin is read there. A lead does not create infinite DC gain, it does not cancel a right-half-plane zero, and its own magnitude usually moves the crossover, which is why the margin is checked again.

questions.prompt: A lead has its pole three times farther from the origin than its zero. The peak phase it can add, in degrees, is
questions.explanation: With \(\alpha = 3\), \(\sin\phi_m = (\alpha-1)/(\alpha+1) = 1/2\), so \(\phi_m = 30\) degrees. Using \(\alpha\) itself, 3, as a degree measure has no meaning. The formula \((\alpha-1)/(\alpha+1)\) is the sine of the angle, not the angle. A lag of the same ratio would contribute a negative phase.

questions.prompt: A lead zero is at \(4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and its pole is at \(16\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The frequency of peak phase, in rad/s, is
questions.explanation: The peak is at the geometric mean \(\sqrt{4 \cdot 16} = 8\). The arithmetic mean \((4+16)/2 = 10\) is not the center of a Bode lead. The difference \(16-4 = 12\) is the gap between the corners, not the frequency of the bump.

questions.prompt: A lead zero is at \(z > 0\) and the pole is at \(p > 0\), both measured in rad/s. Write the frequency of peak phase, in the names z and p.
questions.explanation: Peak lead sits at the geometric mean \(\sqrt{z p}\). The arithmetic mean \((z+p)/2\) is a different average and is not where \(\phi_m\) occurs. The ratio \(p/z\) is the lead ratio \(\alpha\), not a frequency.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where you want crossover, the plant magnitude is \(0.25\). The compensator magnitude that makes \(|L| = 1\) there is
questions.explanation: \(|L| = |C|\,|P|\). Setting that to 1 gives \(|C| = 1/0.25 = 4\). Using the plant magnitude itself, 0.25, would leave \(|L| = 0.0625\). Adding 1 to the plant magnitude is not the required compensator.

questions.prompt: Put these loop-shaping steps in the order you would do them.
questions.explanation: The plant's margin tells you how much phase to buy. The lead is then centered where you want to cross, and the gain is what places the crossing there. Lag and PI come after, below the new crossover, so they do not spend the phase you just added. The last reading is mandatory because every block can move the crossing.

questions.figure_alt: A lead block followed by a plant block.
steps: Read the uncompensated crossover and phase margin.
Choose a lead ratio and center its phase bump on the intended crossover.
Set the gain so the loop crosses over inside that bump.
Add lag or PI below crossover only if the low-frequency gain is still short.
Read the margins again at the crossover you actually got.

questions.prompt: A designer writes this argument about a lead. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The phase bump is local. A decade below crossover, the lead's phase has already fallen well below its peak, so the margin at \(8\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) barely changes. The first two steps are the right readings, and the last step is why you recompute the margin after the gain moves the crossing.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 186" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>magnitude that steepens, then steepens again</title><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="300" y2="156"/><polygon points="300,156 293.6,158.7 293.6,153.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="50" y2="30"/><polygon points="50,30 52.7,36.4 47.3,36.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="300" y="172" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">log ω</text><text x="54" y="26" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">|H| dB</text><polyline points="58,42 150,86 268,142" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="96" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−20</text><text x="188" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−40</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A magnitude sketch that falls, then falls more steeply.
steps: The plant crosses over at \(8\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) with phase \(-150^\circ\), so the phase margin is \(30^\circ\).
A lead can add \(40^\circ\) at the geometric mean of its zero and pole.
Centering that mean at \(0.8\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), a decade below the crossover, adds the full \(40^\circ\) to the phase margin.
The lead's magnitude also moves the crossover, so the margin has to be read again after the gain is set.
reasons: The phase bump is local, so a center a decade below crossover does not deliver the peak lead at crossover.
A phase of \(-150^\circ\) is already unstable, so the margin is not \(30^\circ\).
Lead magnitude cannot move a crossover.

questions.prompt: A lag \((s+1)/(5s+1)\) is placed well below crossover in order to
options: add its peak phase at the crossover
lower the high-frequency loop gain while keeping the DC gain
cancel a right-half-plane pole of the plant
make the slope at crossover steeper by adding a zero there
questions.explanation: The DC gain of this lag is 1 and the high-frequency gain is \(1/5\), so it can drop the crossover into a friendlier phase region without giving up the low-frequency gain. Its phase is negative, a penalty, not a bump you want at crossover. It does not cancel an unstable pole, and its zero is the higher corner, not a zero parked at crossover.

questions.prompt: Which of these are lead networks, with both corners in the open left half-plane and the zero closer to the origin?
questions.explanation: \((s+2)/(s+10)\) and \((s+1)/(s+4)\) each put the zero at a smaller magnitude than the pole, and both corners are in the left half-plane. \((s+10)/(s+2)\) is the same corners swapped, which is a lag. \((s-3)/(s+9)\) has a right-half-plane zero, which adds lag rather than lead.

questions.prompt: The lag is \((s+1)/(5s+1)\). Far above both corners, its magnitude approaches
questions.explanation: The high-frequency gain is the ratio of the leading coefficients, \(1/5 = 0.2\). The DC gain is 1, which is the value far below both corners. The corner ratio 5 is how many times smaller the high-frequency gain is, not the gain itself.

questions.prompt: After the gain is raised so that crossover falls at the lead's geometric center,
options: the closed-loop poles stay at the open-loop locations
sensor noise is removed by the lead zero
phase margin must be read at the new crossover, not the old one
a lag is no longer allowed anywhere in the loop
questions.explanation: Phase margin is the gap from \(-180^\circ\) at whatever frequency now has \(|L| = 1\). Moving the crossing moves that frequency. The lead does not freeze the closed-loop poles at the open-loop poles, it does not filter every sensor noise, and a lag below the new crossover is still a normal second step.

questions.prompt: A PI factor \(K_p(s + 1/\tau_i)/s\), used as part of a loop shape,
options: is identical to a lead whose pole and zero have been swapped
removes sensor noise above the crossover
cancels the plant's slowest stable pole for every \(\tau_i\)
puts a pole at the origin, so a constant error integrates away, and a zero that limits the phase loss at crossover
questions.explanation: The pole at the origin makes the low-frequency loop gain infinite, which is what removes a constant error. The zero at \(-1/\tau_i\) stops that pole from still costing \(90^\circ\) at crossover, provided the zero is placed below the crossing. Swapping a lead's corners produces a lag, not a PI. The PI zero is not a noise filter, and it cancels a plant pole only when you deliberately set \(\tau_i\) to that pole.
